chunks: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — and he had been asked about 'the First' and 'the Last' — and he said: 'The First' means not from a first before Him nor from a beginning preceding Him; and 'the Last' means not from an end-point in the way that is understood from the attributes of created beings. But He is eternal — First, Last — He has always been and will never cease, without a beginning and without an end. Temporal origination does not befall Him, nor does He change from one state to another. He is the Creator of all things.

key_terms.الآخر: al-Akhir — 'The Last': divine name affirming God's endless, unconditioned permanence beyond all created things
key_terms.الأوّل: al-Awwal — 'The First': divine name affirming God's unoriginated, causeless priority over all existence
key_terms.الحدوث: al-Huduth — Temporal origination/contingency; what happens to created things but not to God
key_terms.خالق كل شيء: Creator of all things — affirming God's absolute creative sovereignty
key_terms.قديم: Qadim — Pre-eternal, existing without a temporal beginning; a key theological term in kalam

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Sadiq say about the meaning of the divine names al-Awwal and al-Akhir?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked about the divine names 'al-Awwal' (the First) and 'al-Akhir' (the Last) as they appear in the Quran (57:3). He clarifies that these names must not be understood in the creaturely sense — they do not imply that God had a prior first before Him, nor an end-point after Him. Rather, they affirm His absolute, self-subsisting eternity: He is qadim (pre-existent without cause), unchanging, not subject to temporal occurrence (huduth), and the Creator of all things. This hadith is a cornerstone of Shia kalam (theology) refuting anthropomorphic or creaturely understandings of divine attributes.
